p.src: Now Cao Cao, intending to send Yu Jin to relieve Fan Castle, asked which of his generals dared serve as vanguard. One man at once volunteered. Cao Cao looked and saw that it was Pang De. Cao Cao was delighted and said, “Guan has struck awe throughout the realm and has yet to meet his match; now that he meets a man of your renown, he will truly have a formidable foe.” He therefore appointed Yu Jin General Who Subdues the South and Pang De Chief Vanguard Who Subdues the West, raised seven armies, and sent them toward Fan Castle. These seven armies were composed entirely of hardy men from the north. Two officers commanded them: one named Dong Heng and the other Dong Chao. That day they brought all their subordinate commanders to pay respects to Yu Jin. Dong Heng said, “General, you now command seven powerful armies to deliver Fan Castle from peril, and victory must be assured; yet by making Pang De the vanguard, are you not risking the whole undertaking?” Startled, Yu Jin asked why. Dong Heng said, “Pang De was formerly Ma Chao’s lieutenant and surrendered to Wei only under compulsion. His former lord is now in Shu, holding rank among the ‘Five Tiger Generals’; moreover, his elder brother Pang Rou also holds office in Western Sichuan. To make him vanguard now would be like pouring oil on a fire in hopes of extinguishing it. Why not inform the King of Wei and have another man appointed?”

p.src: On hearing this, Yu Jin went to Cao Cao’s residence that very night and reported it. Cao Cao saw the point and immediately summoned Pang De before the steps, ordering him to surrender the vanguard’s seal. Pang De was greatly alarmed. “I long only to exert myself in Your Majesty’s service. Why will you not employ me?” Cao Cao said, “I myself harbor no suspicions. But Ma Chao is now in Western Sichuan, and your brother Pang Rou is there as well; both serve Liu Bei. Though I do not doubt you, what can be done about the multitude of voices?” Hearing this, Pang De removed his cap and repeatedly struck his forehead against the ground until his face was covered in blood. He pleaded, “Since surrendering to Your Majesty from Hanzhong, I have ever been grateful for your great favor. Even if my liver and brains were smeared upon the earth, I could not repay it. Why should Your Majesty doubt me? In former days, when I was in my native place, I lived with my elder brother. His wife was exceedingly wicked, and in a drunken fit I killed her. My brother hates me to the marrow of his bones and swore never to see me again; all affection between us is severed. My former lord Ma Chao had courage but no strategy; defeated in war and stripped of his lands, he fled alone into Sichuan. Now he and I each serve our own lord, and our former bond is ended. Grateful as I am for Your Majesty’s gracious treatment, how could I dare conceive disloyalty? I beg Your Majesty to judge my heart.” Cao Cao then helped Pang De to his feet and comforted him, saying, “I have always known your loyalty and honor. What I said before was only to set everyone’s mind at ease. Strive now to win merit. If you do not fail me, I shall certainly never fail you.”

p.src: Pang De bowed his thanks and returned home, where he ordered a craftsman to make a wooden coffin. The next day he invited his friends to a banquet and set the coffin in the hall. All his relatives and friends were startled at the sight and asked, “Why use this inauspicious object when you are setting out to war, General?” Raising his cup, Pang De told them, “I have received great favor from the King of Wei and have sworn to repay him with my death. Now I go to Fan Castle to fight Guan to the death. If I cannot kill him, he will surely kill me. Even if he does not kill me, I shall take my own life. Therefore I have prepared this coffin beforehand, to show there can be no return empty-handed.” They all sighed in wonder. Pang De summoned his wife, Lady Li, and his son, Pang Hui, and told his wife, “I now go forth as vanguard, and honor requires that I give my life upon the battlefield. If I die, raise our son with the greatest care. Our son bears extraordinary features; when he grows up, he will surely avenge me.” His wife and son wept bitterly as they bade him farewell, and Pang De ordered the coffin carried along. As he was departing, he told his subordinate officers, “I now go to fight Guan to the death. If Guan kills me, quickly retrieve my body and place it in this coffin. But if I kill Guan, I shall take his head, place it in this coffin, and return to present it to the King of Wei.” All five hundred of his men said, “With such loyalty and courage in our general, how could we fail to give our utmost in your aid?” Thereupon they led the army onward. Someone reported these words to Cao Cao. Cao Cao rejoiced. “With Pang De so loyal and courageous, what have I to fear?” Jia Xu said, “Pang De relies upon the courage of hot blood and intends to fight Guan to the death. Privately, I fear for him.” Cao Cao agreed and hastily sent an order warning Pang De: “Guan possesses both wisdom and valor; you must on no account underestimate him. Attack if he can be taken; if he cannot, you must defend with care.” On receiving the command, Pang De said to the generals, “Why does the King hold Guan in such high regard? I expect on this expedition to shatter the reputation he has built over thirty years.” Yu Jin said, “The King of Wei’s words must be obeyed.” Pang De spiritedly hurried the army forward to Fan Castle, flaunting his might amid the clang of gongs and thunder of drums.

p.src: Meanwhile, Lord Guan was seated in his tent when a scout suddenly galloped in to report: “Cao Cao has appointed Yu Jin commander and sent him here with seven armies of picked, sturdy troops. The vanguard commander, Pang De, has a wooden coffin carried before his army. He has uttered insolent words and sworn to fight you to the death. His troops are now only thirty li from the city.” At these words Lord Guan’s face changed abruptly, and his magnificent beard streamed as he cried in fury, “Every hero under Heaven who hears my name fears me and submits. How dare that whelp Pang De hold me in contempt! Let Guan Ping continue the attack on Fan Castle. I shall go myself and behead this brute to vent my wrath!” Guan Ping said, “Father, one of Mount Tai’s weight should not contend for height with a stubborn stone. Your unworthy son begs to fight Pang De in your place.” Lord Guan said, “Go and make the attempt. I shall follow shortly to support you.”

p.src: Guan Ping left the tent, took up his blade, mounted his horse, and led his troops out to meet Pang De. The two battle lines formed opposite each other. In the Wei camp, four great white characters on a black banner read: “Pang De of Nan’an.” Pang De, in a blue robe and silver armor, wielding a steel blade and mounted on a white horse, stood before the battle line. Five hundred soldiers followed close behind him, and several foot soldiers came forth carrying the wooden coffin on their shoulders. Guan Ping reviled Pang De: “Traitor who betrayed his lord!” Pang De asked his men, “Who is that?” Someone replied, “That is Lord Guan’s adopted son, Guan Ping.” Pang De called out, “By command of the King of Wei, I have come to take your father’s head! You are no more than a mangy brat; I will not kill you! Call your father here at once!” Guan Ping flew into a rage, spurred his horse, brandished his blade, and charged at Pang De. Pang De met him with his blade held crosswise. They fought thirty bouts without either gaining the advantage, then both sides withdrew to rest.

p.src: Word had already been carried to Lord Guan. Enraged, he ordered Liao Hua to attack Fan Castle and came in person to meet Pang De. Guan Ping met him and reported that he had fought Pang De without either side prevailing. Lord Guan immediately rode forth with his blade held crosswise and shouted, “Guan Yunchang is here! Pang De, why do you not come quickly to your death?” As the drums thundered, Pang De rode out and said, “By command of the King of Wei, I have come expressly to take your head! Lest you doubt me, I have prepared a coffin here. If you fear death, dismount and surrender at once!” Lord Guan cursed him: “What can a mere brute like you accomplish? It is a pity to stain my Green Dragon Blade by beheading a rat like you!” He spurred his horse, flourished his blade, and charged at Pang De. Pang De whirled his blade and met the attack. The two generals fought more than a hundred bouts, their vigor only mounting. Both armies watched in utter fascination. Fearing harm might befall Pang De, the Wei army hurriedly sounded the gong to withdraw. Guan Ping, fearing for his aged father, also hastened to sound the recall. The two generals each withdrew. Back in camp, Pang De told the others, “People call Lord Guan a hero; only today do I believe it.” While he was still speaking, Yu Jin arrived. After they had exchanged greetings, Yu Jin said, “I hear you fought Lord Guan for more than a hundred bouts without gaining any advantage. Why not withdraw for now and avoid him?” Pang De answered indignantly, “The King of Wei appointed you commander-in-chief. Why are you so fainthearted? Tomorrow I shall fight Guan to the death. I swear I will not retreat or evade him!” Yu Jin dared not oppose him and returned.

p.src: Guan Yu returned to camp and said to Guan Ping, “Pang De is thoroughly skilled with the saber; he is truly a match for me.” Guan Ping replied, “As the common saying goes, ‘A newborn calf does not fear the tiger.’ Even if Father should slay this man, he is but a lowly soldier from the western Qiang; but should any mishap befall you, it would ill repay the great trust my uncle placed in you.” Guan Yu said, “Unless I kill this man, how can I avenge this humiliation? My mind is made up. Say no more!” The next day, he mounted his horse and led his troops forward. Pang De likewise led out his troops to meet him. When the two formations had drawn up face-to-face, both generals rode forth; without exchanging a word, they charged into combat. After more than fifty bouts, Pang De wheeled his horse, trailed his saber behind him, and fled. Guan Yu pursued him from behind. Fearing some mishap, Guan Ping followed in pursuit. Guan Yu shouted abuse: “Pang De, you rogue! You mean to use the trailing-saber ruse. Do you think I fear you?” Pang De had only feigned the trailing-saber maneuver. He hooked his saber onto the saddle bow, secretly drew his carved bow, nocked an arrow, and shot. Guan Ping’s keen eyes saw Pang De draw his bow, and he cried, “Traitorous general, do not loose a hidden arrow!” Guan Yu opened his eyes wide to look, but at the twang of the bowstring the arrow was already upon him; he could not dodge in time, and it struck him squarely in the left arm. Guan Ping galloped up and rescued his father, taking him back to camp.

p.src: Pang De reined his horse around and came pursuing with saber whirling, when suddenly the gongs in his own camp sounded furiously. Fearing that something had gone wrong in the rear, Pang De hastily turned back. In fact, when Yu Jin saw Pang De shoot Guan Yu, he feared Pang De would win great merit and eclipse his own prestige, so he had sounded the gong to recall the army. Pang De rode back and asked why the recall had been sounded. Yu Jin said, “The King of Wei warned us that Guan Yu possesses both wisdom and valor. Though he was struck by an arrow, I feared it might be a ruse, and therefore sounded the recall.” Pang De said, “Had you not recalled the army, I would already have beheaded him.” Yu Jin replied, “Haste makes poor progress. We must proceed against him gradually.” Pang De did not understand Yu Jin’s intention and could only lament bitterly.

p.src: Meanwhile, Guan Yu returned to camp and had the arrowhead removed. Fortunately, the arrow had not gone deep, and wound medicine was applied. Guan Yu bitterly hated Pang De and said to his generals, “I swear to avenge this arrow wound!” The generals replied, “General, rest for several days first. It will not be too late to fight him afterward.” The next day, a man reported that Pang De had led out troops to challenge them. Guan Yu at once wished to go out and fight. His generals dissuaded and restrained him. Pang De ordered his soldiers to hurl insults. Guan Ping guarded the pass and instructed the generals not to report this to Guan Yu. After Pang De had challenged them for more than ten days without anyone coming forth, he consulted Yu Jin: “Plainly Guan Yu’s arrow wound has flared up, leaving him unable to move; we should seize this opportunity, unite the Seven Armies, and storm his camp in one rush. Then we can lift the siege of Fancheng.” Yu Jin feared Pang De would succeed, so he merely invoked the King of Wei’s warning and refused to move the troops. Pang De repeatedly urged an attack, but Yu Jin would never consent; instead, he moved the Seven Armies beyond the mountain pass and encamped against the hills, ten li north of Fancheng. Yu Jin personally led troops to block the main road and ordered Pang De to station his forces behind the valley, preventing him from advancing and winning merit.

p.src: Meanwhile, Guan Ping was delighted to see that Guan Yu’s arrow wound had healed. Suddenly he heard that Yu Jin had moved the Seven Armies to encamp north of Fancheng. Not knowing what he intended, Guan Ping reported it to Guan Yu. Guan Yu mounted his horse and rode with several horsemen to survey the scene from a high mound. He saw that the banners atop Fancheng were in disarray and its soldiers were panicking; in a mountain valley ten li north of the city, troops and horses were encamped; and he also saw that the Xiang River was flowing with tremendous force. After watching for some time, he summoned a local guide and asked, “What is the name of that valley ten li north of Fancheng?” The guide replied, “It is Zengkou Valley.” Guan Yu rejoiced and said, “Yu Jin is certain to be captured by me.” The soldiers asked, “How do you know this, General?” Guan Yu said, “Once the ‘fish’ enter the ‘mouth of the net,’ how can they last long?” The generals did not believe him. Guan Yu returned to his own camp. It was now autumn, in the eighth month, and torrential rain fell for several days. Guan Yu ordered boats and rafts prepared and all equipment needed on the water made ready. Guan Ping asked, “Since we are confronting them on land, what need have we of water equipment?” Guan Yu said, “This is beyond your understanding. Yu Jin has not stationed his Seven Armies on broad, level ground, but has massed them in the narrow and perilous confines of Zengkou Valley; now the autumn rains continue without cease, and the Xiang River is certain to overflow; I have already sent men to dam every outlet. When the waters rise, we shall embark from the high ground and release the flood in one great surge. Then all the troops at Fancheng and Zengkou Valley will become food for fish and turtles.” Guan Ping bowed in admiration.

p.src: Meanwhile, the Wei army was encamped at Zengkou Valley, where heavy rain fell without cease for days on end. The supervising officer Cheng He came to see Yu Jin and said, “The army is stationed at the mouth of the valley, where the ground is extremely low; although there is an earthen hill, it lies some distance from camp. Now the autumn rains continue without end, and the soldiers are suffering greatly. Recently, men have reported that the Jingzhou troops have moved to high ground and are also preparing battle rafts at the mouth of the Han River; should the river overflow, our army will be in peril. We must make plans without delay.” Yu Jin rebuked him: “Wretch! Are you trying to unsettle the morale of my army? The next man who speaks such words will be beheaded!” Cheng He withdrew in shame, then went to Pang De and told him what had happened. Pang De said, “What you have observed is entirely correct. Since General Yu refuses to move the army, tomorrow I shall move my own troops and encamp elsewhere.” They had just settled their plan when, that very night, wind and rain broke forth with tremendous violence. As Pang De sat in his tent, he heard what seemed like ten thousand horses stampeding and the thunder of war drums shaking the earth. Greatly alarmed, Pang De rushed from his tent, mounted his horse, and looked about. From every direction, floodwaters were suddenly surging in; the Seven Armies scattered in confusion, and countless men were swept away by the waves; even on level ground the water stood more than a zhang deep. Yu Jin, Pang De, and the other generals each climbed a small hill to escape the flood. By daybreak, Guan Yu and all his generals came aboard great ships, waving banners and raising a thunderous clamor. Yu Jin saw that there was no road of escape in any direction and that only fifty or sixty men remained around him. Knowing he could not flee, he called out that he wished to surrender. Guan Yu ordered them all stripped of their armor and taken into custody aboard the ships; then he went to capture Pang De.

u.src: Meanwhile, the Wei army was encamped at Zengkou Valley, where heavy rain fell without cease for days on end.
The supervising officer Cheng He came to see Yu Jin and said, “The army is stationed at the mouth of the valley, where the ground is extremely low;
although there is an earthen hill, it lies some distance from camp. Now the autumn rains continue without end, and the soldiers are suffering greatly.
Recently, men have reported that the Jingzhou troops have moved to high ground and are also preparing battle rafts at the mouth of the Han River;
should the river overflow, our army will be in peril.
We must make plans without delay.”
Yu Jin rebuked him: “Wretch! Are you trying to unsettle the morale of my army?
The next man who speaks such words will be beheaded!”
Cheng He withdrew in shame, then went to Pang De and told him what had happened.
Pang De said, “What you have observed is entirely correct.
Since General Yu refuses to move the army, tomorrow I shall move my own troops and encamp elsewhere.”
They had just settled their plan when, that very night, wind and rain broke forth with tremendous violence.
As Pang De sat in his tent, he heard what seemed like ten thousand horses stampeding and the thunder of war drums shaking the earth.
Greatly alarmed, Pang De rushed from his tent, mounted his horse, and looked about. From every direction, floodwaters were suddenly surging in;
the Seven Armies scattered in confusion, and countless men were swept away by the waves;
even on level ground the water stood more than a zhang deep.
Yu Jin, Pang De, and the other generals each climbed a small hill to escape the flood.
By daybreak, Guan Yu and all his generals came aboard great ships, waving banners and raising a thunderous clamor.
Yu Jin saw that there was no road of escape in any direction and that only fifty or sixty men remained around him. Knowing he could not flee, he called out that he wished to surrender.
Guan Yu ordered them all stripped of their armor and taken into custody aboard the ships; then he went to capture Pang De.

p.src: At this time, Pang De, the two Dongs, and Cheng He stood upon the embankment with five hundred foot soldiers, all without armor or protective clothing. When Pang De saw Lord Guan approaching, he showed no fear at all, but strode boldly forward to engage him. Lord Guan had the boats surround them on every side, and his soldiers loosed their arrows together, killing more than half the Wei troops. Seeing that their plight was desperate, Dong Heng and Dong Chao said to Pang De, “More than half our men have fallen, and there is no escape in any direction. We had better surrender.” Pang De cried in fury, “I have received great favor from the King of Wei. How could I ever abase my honor before another?” He thereupon personally beheaded Dong Heng and Dong Chao before the others, then shouted sternly, “Let these two serve as an example to anyone who speaks of surrender again!” At this, they all exerted themselves to resist the enemy. They fought from daybreak until noon, their valor and strength only redoubling. Lord Guan pressed the assault urgently from all four sides, while arrows and stones fell like rain. Pang De ordered his soldiers to meet the enemy with close-combat weapons. Pang De looked back at Cheng He and said, “I have heard it said: ‘A valiant general does not shrink from death to steal his safety, nor does a brave man destroy his honor to preserve his life.’ Today is the day of my death. You too must strive and fight to the death.” Obeying the command, Cheng He charged forward, but an arrow from Lord Guan struck him and sent him tumbling into the water. All the troops surrendered; Pang De alone continued to fight with all his might. Just then, several dozen men from Jingzhou came toward the embankment in a small boat. Pang De gripped his sword and leapt aboard; in an instant he had killed more than ten of them, while the rest abandoned the boat and plunged into the water to escape with their lives. Holding his sword in one hand and working a short oar with the other, Pang De sought to make his escape toward Fan Castle. But from upstream came a general poling a great raft. He rammed and overturned the small boat, throwing Pang De into the water. The general aboard leapt into the water, captured Pang De alive, and hauled him onto the vessel. When everyone looked, they saw that Pang De’s captor was none other than Zhou Cang. Zhou Cang had always been a strong swimmer, and after living in Jingzhou for several years had become still more at home in the water; added to this, his strength was prodigious, and thus he captured Pang De. The Seven Armies under Yu Jin’s command all perished in the flood. Those who could swim reckoned that there was no way of escape and surrendered as well. A later poet wrote:

p.src: Lord Guan returned to the high ground, entered his command tent, and took his seat. The executioners escorted Yu Jin before him. Yu Jin prostrated himself on the ground, begging for mercy and his life. Lord Guan said, “How dared you oppose me?” Yu Jin replied, “I was dispatched by command from above and had no choice of my own. I pray that you, my lord, will show mercy; I swear to repay you even at the cost of my life.” Stroking his beard, Lord Guan laughed and said, “For me to kill you would be no different from slaughtering a dog or swine—it would only soil the blade and axe!” He ordered that Yu Jin be bound and sent to the main prison in Jingzhou to await judgment, saying, “When I return, I shall decide how else to deal with him.” Once this disposition had been carried out, Lord Guan ordered Pang De brought before him. Pang De stood without kneeling, his brows raised and eyes blazing with anger. Lord Guan said, “Your elder brother is now in Hanzhong; and your former lord, Ma Chao, is also serving as a great general in Shu; why did you not surrender sooner?” Pang De cried in fury, “I would sooner die beneath the blade than surrender to you!” He continued to hurl abuse without cease. Enraged, Lord Guan shouted for the executioners to drag him out and behead him. Pang De stretched out his neck and accepted his execution. Lord Guan admired him and had him buried. Then, while the floodwaters had yet to recede, he boarded the warships once more and led his officers of every rank to attack Fan Castle.

p.src: Now all around Fan Castle, white-crested waves surged to the heavens, and the flood grew ever more violent; the city walls gradually became waterlogged and collapsed. Men and women carried earth and moved bricks, yet could not fill the breaches. Every one of Cao’s generals lost heart and hurried to report to Cao Ren. Cao Ren said, “The peril we face today cannot be remedied by force. Before the enemy arrives, we should take boats and escape by night. Though we lose the city, we may yet preserve our lives.” While they were deliberating, and just as they were about to prepare boats and flee, Man Chong remonstrated, “You must not. How could a mountain flood that came so suddenly endure for long? In less than ten days, it will surely subside of itself. Though Lord Guan has not yet attacked the city, he has already dispatched another general to Jia. The reason he dares not advance rashly is that he fears our army may strike his rear. If we now abandon the city and depart, all the land south of the Yellow River will cease to belong to the state. I beg you, General, to hold this city firmly and make it our bulwark.” Cao Ren clasped his hands in thanks and said, “But for your counsel, Boning, I would nearly have ruined our great cause.” He then mounted his white horse, rode up onto the wall, assembled his generals, and swore before them, “I have received the King of Wei’s command to defend this city. Anyone who speaks of abandoning the city and leaving shall be beheaded!” All the generals declared, “We are willing to defend it to the death!” Cao Ren was delighted and had several hundred bows and crossbows set up upon the walls. The soldiers kept watch day and night, not daring to relax their vigilance. The inhabitants, old and young alike, carried earth and stones to repair the city walls. Within ten days, the floodwaters gradually receded.

p.src: Since capturing the Wei general Yu Jin and the others, Lord Guan’s might had shaken the realm, and none heard of it without alarm. Presently, his second son, Guan Xing, came to the encampment to pay his respects. Lord Guan ordered Guan Xing to carry to Chengdu the documents recording the officers’ achievements, present them to the King of Hanzhong, and request promotion for each of them. Guan Xing bowed farewell to his father and went directly to Chengdu.

p.src: Now Lord Guan divided off half his forces and sent them straight to Jia. He himself led the remaining troops in attacking Fan Castle from every side. That day Lord Guan went in person to the north gate. Sitting his horse, he raised his whip, pointed, and called out, “You pack of rats! If you do not surrender at once, what are you waiting for?” While he was still speaking, Cao Ren, watching from the gate tower, saw that Lord Guan wore only a breastplate, with his green robe hanging loosely and exposing one shoulder. He hastily summoned five hundred archers and crossbowmen and ordered them all to loose at once. As Lord Guan hastily reined his horse around, a crossbow bolt struck his right arm, and he pitched from the saddle. Indeed:
